questions.prompt: Decide whether \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) is invertible using its determinant.
questions.answer: Compute the determinant: \(2\cdot4\) - \(1\cdot3\) = 8 - 3 = 5. Since the determinant is non-zero, the matrix is invertible.

questions.prompt: Decide whether \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\) is invertible using its determinant.
questions.answer: Compute the determinant: \(1\cdot4\) - \(2\cdot2\) = 4 - 4 = 0. A square matrix with determinant 0 is not invertible. Therefore the matrix is not invertible.

questions.prompt: If A is \(3\times 3\) and \(\det(A)\) = -7, what can you conclude about \(Ax=b\) for every b in \(\mathbb R^3\)?
questions.answer: Since \(\det(A)\) is non-zero, A is invertible. Therefore for every b in \(\mathbb R^3\), the system \(Ax=b\) has exactly one solution, namely x = \(A^{-1}\)b.

questions.prompt: If \(\det(A)\) = 0 for a square matrix A, what can you conclude about \(Ax=0\)?
questions.answer: If \(\det(A)\) = 0, then A is not invertible. By the invertible matrix theorem, the homogeneous system \(Ax=0\) has a non-trivial solution. It also has the trivial solution \(x=0\), so it has infinitely many solutions when A is square.

questions.prompt: Find all real t such that \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t&2\\8&t\end{pmatrix}\) is invertible.
questions.answer: A is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero. Compute \(\det(A)\) = \(t^2\) - 16. This is non-zero when \(t^2\) != 16, so t != 4 and t != -4. Therefore A is invertible for all real t except \(t=4\) and \(t=-4\).

questions.prompt: A triangular \(4\times 4\) matrix has diagonal entries 1, -2, 3, and 0. Is it invertible?
questions.answer: The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries. Here the product is 1*(-2)*\(3\cdot0\) = 0. Since the determinant is zero, the matrix is not invertible.

questions.prompt: If A and B are invertible square matrices, explain why \(AB\) is invertible using determinants.
questions.answer: If A and B are invertible, then \(\det(A)\) and \(\det(B)\) are both non-zero. The product rule gives \(\det(\(AB\))\) = \(\det(A)\)\(\det(B)\). A product of two non-zero numbers is non-zero, so \(\det(\(AB\))\) != 0. Therefore \(AB\) is invertible.

questions.prompt: Suppose \(\det(A)\) = 5 and \(\det(B)\) = 0 for square matrices of the same size. Is \(AB\) invertible?
questions.answer: Use the product rule: \(\det(\(AB\))\) = \(\det(A)\)\(\det(B)\) = \(5\cdot0\) = 0. Since \(\det(\(AB\))\) = 0, the product \(AB\) is not invertible.

questions.prompt: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\0&1&4\\0&0&5\end{pmatrix}\), decide invertibility without row reducing.
questions.answer: A is upper triangular, so \(\det(A)\) is the product of its diagonal entries: \(1\cdot1\)*5 = 5. Since the determinant is non-zero, A is invertible.

questions.prompt: A learner says a matrix with a negative determinant is not invertible. Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: Invertibility depends on whether the determinant is zero, not whether it is positive. Any non-zero determinant, positive or negative, means the matrix is invertible. For example, \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\) has determinant -1 and is invertible. The learner confused negative with zero.
